newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Opposition stages massive New Year celebration.
newsitem.headline: Opposition stages massive New Year celebration.

text.p: Thousands of opposition supporters held a huge New Year's rally to the din of drums and whistles in a central Belgrade square to demand a democratic Serbia, hours after President Slobodan Milosevic ignored protests against election fraud.

The large central square was more tightly packed even than at the height of anti-Milosevic demonstrations in December when the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition drew up to 250,000 people to rallies.
Streets leading to the square were also packed solid with people to the despair of traffic police, the only security forces visibly present in the sub-zero temperatures.

Zajedno organized the street party with alarm clocks and a cacophony of bells it says will be tolling for Milosevic on the stroke of midnight telling the communist-turned-socialist that his time was running out.

The street spectacle took advantage of Belgrade's traditional enthusiasm for celebrating the New Year to help maintain the enthusiasm of Zajedno's supporters whose ranks have dwindled since snowy, sub-zero weather set in a week ago.

It is also a way around an Interior Ministry ban on marches that disrupt traffic that has driven the protests off the city streets and onto a narrow pedestrian mall thanks to thousands of heavily armed riot police.
The din from truphets, drums, whistles and fireworks was immense.
The massive turnout was a slap to Milosevic who only hours earlier wished his people a happy New Year, promising market reforms in a veiled attempt to appease the West.

"The coming year will be a year of reforms -- major ownership and structural changes which should make possible an affirmation of all motivating elements in a market economy," he said in a statement broadcast by Serbian state televivision.

Milosevic only obliquely referred to the political crisis that began after his ruling socialists reversed local election results which awarded control of 15 of the biggest towns in Serbia, including Belgrade, to the opposition.
The fraud has sparked 44 days of mass demonstrations in Belgrade and dozens of other towns by students and opposition supporters demanding respect for democracy.
A report by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) recommends that Milosevic fully accept the opposition victories.
Milosevic's deliberate snub poured cold water over hopes that the issue could be resolved in the near future.

Before midnight, protesting Belgrade students sneaked past Milosevic's feared security forces and after three attempts foiled by hundreds of riot police managed to reach Milosevic's home in the elite residential district of Dedinje.
A group of some 20 student representatives, camera crews and reporters took a trolley-bus to Dedinje from the city centre and then walked up the street to Milosevic's home.
"The four policemen standing outside Milosevic's home were stunned when they saw students," a witness said.
"One of them told the students they could not pass by under any circumstances, so they shook hands with him and wished them a happy New Year," the witness said.
Later some 5,000 students staged a "happening" in a Belgrade square as part of the New Year celebrations.
Six of them shut themselves in a cage while a magician performed a trick with vanishing ballots in a box ridiculing the ruling socialists for their election fraud.
